Fishing remained the main trade, but tourism grew each summer, and shopkeepers began to depend on visitors who arrived on the morning train. By 1910 the council had paved the promenade, built a bandstand, and opened a small museum in the old customs house. The harbour itself silted up after a storm in 1923, and the fishing fleet moved west to a deeper bay. Hotels replaced the warehouses along the quay, and the population doubled over the next thirty years. Historians disagree about how much the new pier mattered, though most agree that the town's fortunes rose and fell with the railway timetable. A fire in 1958 destroyed the bandstand and much of the eastern promenade, and the museum closed within a decade. Restoration began in the 1980s, funded partly by a national heritage grant and partly by local donations. Volunteers rebuilt the bandstand from old photographs and reopened the museum in the customs house. Over the past two decades, the waterfront has become the centre of a small but steady tourist trade. Fishing boats still leave the bay before dawn, and the morning auction on the quay draws visitors throughout the summer. The council now limits new building along the seafront, and the railway, converted to a heritage line, carries passengers between the town and the hills each weekend. A second museum, devoted to the fishing fleet, opened in a former warehouse in 2004. Its exhibits include nets, brass compasses, and photographs of the families who worked the boats for generations. School groups visit on weekdays, and on summer evenings the quay hosts concerts that draw crowds from the surrounding villages. Plans for a new sea wall are debated every winter, when storms push water across the lower streets. Most residents accept the inconvenience because the harbour remains the reason visitors come.
